title: The Confession of Little Hawley
premise: When Kestrel Dunmore exhumes town founder Ambrose Hawley for a land dispute, the coffin is empty—and inside lies a child's shoe and a confession note dated thirty years ago. As Kestrel digs into the summer of 1994, he uncovers a cover-up involving the town's founding families, a missing boy everyone called 'Little Hawley,' and his own mother's unexplained absence that same year. The alibis unravel to reveal that Ambrose faked his own death decades early, and Kestrel's mother helped bury the truth of what happened to the boy. In the end, Kestreal must choose between prosecuting the last living conspirator—his own father figure, the retired sheriff—or letting Little Hawley's memory finally rest, closing the case by giving the boy a name and a grave.
about_author: Wendell Quintana is a former rural records clerk who spent fifteen years cataloguing small-town deaths before turning to fiction. He writes mysteries about the secrets communities keep in plain sight, drawing on the ledgers, obituaries, and half-truths of the places he has lived.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Kestrel Dunmore's POV. We meet the coroner of Hollow Creek as he prepares an exhumation ordered by a land developer contesting founder Ambrose Hawley's burial plot. Kestrel's pride in knowing every grave establishes his intimacy with the town and his own careful invisibility. Emotional beat: quiet confidence on the edge of disruption.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The coffin comes up light; inside there is no body—only a child's leather shoe and a folded note reading 'Forgive me. He was never here.' The crowd of onlookers goes silent. Kestrel realizes the town's origin story is a fabrication. Emotional beat: vertigo as certainty collapses.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibis
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. He pulls the 1994 archives and finds every record from that summer either missing or suspiciously tidy. The statute of limitations expires in ninety days. He interviews the elderly town clerk, who warns him some doors stay shut for reasons. Emotional beat: first flicker of obsession.

chapters.title: Little Hawley
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, intercut with a 1994 fragment. Town legend says Ambrose raised an orphaned nephew, 'Little Hawley,' who vanished one August night. No death certificate exists. Kestrel begins mapping who benefited from the boy's erasure. Emotional beat: tenderness toward a forgotten child.

chapters.title: The Sheriff Who Never Retired
chapters.summary: Kestrel visits Ezra Vann, the retired sheriff who signed off on the 1994 disappearance, now living at the edge of town tending bees. Ezra is courteous, evasive, and gives Kestrel a jar of honey and a warning. Emotional beat: unease beneath small-town warmth.

chapters.title: Mother's Summer
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Digging into family papers, he discovers his mother left Hollow Creek for exactly three months in 1994—the same window as the boy's disappearance—and never spoke of it. His sense of self begins to crack. Emotional beat: personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the historical society basement he finds the founders' ledger with pages razored out, and a photograph of Ambrose holding a boy whose face has been scratched away. Someone else has been searching recently—fresh fingerprints in the dust. Emotional beat: dread of being watched.

chapters.title: What Delia Saw
chapters.summary: Delia Marsh's POV (1994 flashback). A teenage girl saw a truck by the old quarry the night Little Hawley vanished and was paid to forget. Present-day Delia, dying of illness, decides she wants to be honest before the end. Emotional beat: guilt seeking absolution.

chapters.title: Honey and Ash
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Delia tells him about the quarry and names three men present that night: Ambrose, Ezra Vann, and Kestrel's own father, Thomas Dunmore. Kestrel refuses to believe it—until he finds his father's old truck in the county impound records. Emotional beat: betrayal blooming.

chapters.title: The Quarry Floor
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. He searches the drained quarry and finds a rusted lunchbox with 'A.H.' scratched inside—Ambrose Hawley, not the boy. The evidence points somewhere unthinkable: the founder staged everything. Emotional beat: the ground shifting under a lifelong identity.

chapters.title: A Man Who Buried Himself
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. County records reveal Ambrose Hawley died officially in 1996—in another state, under another name. The man in the honored grave was a monument, not a person. Kestrel wonders if the whole town is built on a performance. Emotional beat: grief for a false god.

chapters.title: Ezra's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Ezra Vann's POV. Under pressure from Kestrel and his failing conscience, Ezra admits he helped stage the empty coffin in 1994—but claims he did it to protect someone, not Ambrose. He stops short of naming them. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A restored version of the scratched photograph shows the boy standing beside a young woman—Kestrel's mother. Her three-month absence becomes the center of the mystery. Kestrel confronts his father, who shuts down completely. Emotional beat: the past pressing on the present.

chapters.title: Thomas Dunmore's Silence
chapters.summary: Thomas Dunmore's POV (1994 flashback). Thomas found the injured boy by the road after an accident involving Ambrose's car and hid him at his wife's insistence, then helped spread the disappearance story when Ambrose threatened their family. Emotional beat: fear dressed up as protection.

chapters.title: Where the Boy Went
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following his mother's letters to a cousin out west, Kestrel learns Little Hawley lived—raised quietly under a new name until his death two years ago. The statute may expire, but the lie hasn't. Emotional beat: relief tangled with fury.

chapters.title: The Last Conspirator
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Only Ezra remains alive to prosecute, and the developer pushing the exhumation wants the scandal buried to keep building permits alive, offering Kestrel money to stop. Kestrel realizes the town still prefers its myths. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. With days left, Kestrel assembles the full chain: the accident, the hiding, the staged coffin, the erased records. He drafts charges against Ezra and prepares to name his parents' role publicly, knowing it will cost him the town that made him. Emotional beat: resolve hardening into sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Beekeeper's Truth
chapters.summary: Ezra Vann's POV. Ezra confesses fully—not to escape punishment but because Kestrel is the first person in thirty years to ask the right questions. He reveals where the boy's original grave marker was hidden: beneath the founders' monument itself. Emotional beat: release after decades of carrying it alone.

chapters.title: Under the Monument
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At dawn, Kestrel excavates beneath the founders' statue and finds a small marker reading only 'Our Boy.' The town gathers, furious and grieving, as the myth of Ambrose Hawley dies in public. Emotional beat: communal reckoning.

chapters.title: What the Statute Cannot Touch
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The legal clock runs out; Ezra cannot be charged. But Kestrel files the true record anyway—names, dates, the accident—making the archive impossible to razor out again. Justice becomes documentation instead of punishment. Emotional beat: bitter, necessary honesty.

chapters.title: A Name for Little Hawley
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Through the cousin's records, Kestrel recovers the boy's real name—August Hawley—and carves it onto the hidden marker himself. He reads the eulogy no one gave in 1994 while the town listens, some weeping, some walking away. Emotional beat: mourning finally allowed.

chapters.title: Visible
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Weeks later, Kestrel hangs his own name on the coroner's office door for the first time, no longer content to be the town's invisible keeper of graves. He closes the file on Little Hawley—the only case he ever solved by refusing to keep it shut. Emotional beat: belonging earned through truth.
